extracted.intended_audience: readers, critics, and aspiring philosophers/authors (educated readers of philosophical and literary works)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and methodological guidance for reading, evaluating, and producing philosophic/literary prose — including tests of when a reader will profit, how an author should delay rash judgments, and foundational postulates for philosophical construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigorous self-examination before decisive commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Before adopting or publishing a strong doctrinal position (or abandoning received opinion), the individual should 'ascertain with strict self-examination' whether other influences are at work, 'catalogue his scruples, and reduce them to a distinct intelligible form', and be sure he has 'read with a docile mind and favourable dispositions the best and most fundamental works on the subject'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance includes seeking elders or contemporaries who entertained similar scruples and examined them (so one can learn from their experience), delaying irrevocable steps until manhood, knowledge, judgment, and temperance have grown; delay prevents rashness/vanity from alloying decisions. Anti-pattern: precipitately embracing or rejecting opinions without this due self-scrutiny and grounding in fundamental works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid premature or excessive authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Herder (quoted) warns: 'Am sorgfaeltigsten, meiden sie die Autorschaft. Zu frueh oder unmaessig gebraucht, macht sie den Kopf wueste and das Herz leer ... Ein Mensch, der nur lieset um zu druecken, lieset wahrscheinlich uebel; und wer jeden Gedanken, der ihm aufstosst, durch Feder and Presse versendet, hat sie in kurzer Zeit alle versandt, und wird bald ein blosser Diener der Druckerey.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule for writers: do not publish too early or too often; reading only to publish degrades comprehension and originality; sending every passing thought to print leads to becoming a mere servant of the press/printer. Anti-pattern: treating every impression as material for immediate publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for reading baffling authors — presume yourself ignorant of his understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Adage: 'until you understand a writer’s ignorance, presume yourself ignorant of his understanding.' When encountering odd or unintelligible passages, first attempt to understand the writer's grounds and the bodily/psychological causes, rather than assuming intentional falsehood or mere nonsense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a fanatic's supernatural narratives can often be explained psychologically without imputing fraud; with Plato, where some passages are unintelligible, the reader should consider his own lack of access to the author's understanding before dismissing the text as jargon. Anti-pattern: quick contemptuous dismissal of difficult passages as nonsense or jargon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read connectedly or skip — avoid decontextualizing fragments
rubrics_metrics.description: Request to reader: 'either pass over the following chapter altogether, or read the whole connectedly. The fairest part of the most beautiful body will appear deformed and monstrous, if dissevered from its place in the organic whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For delicate subjects, separating supporting ideas from the forms that clothe and modify them can produce a misleading 'skeleton'. Recommendation: don't strip ideas from their contextual forms; read contiguous material to preserve meaning. Anti-pattern: excerpting single passages and judging them divorced from the author's structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for whether a reader will profit from transcendental/philosophic exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reader 'receives as fundamental facts ... the general notions of matter, spirit, soul, body, action, passiveness, time, space, cause and effect, consciousness, perception, memory and habit' and is content to analyse everything into those notions, then 'for him the chapter was not written.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a pre-read test: readers who treat those broad concepts as final elements and are satisfied with reductionist analyses will not benefit from transcendental/philosophy designed to probe beyond spontaneous consciousness. Anti-pattern: approaching transcendental work with the assumption that common elementary notions are the last word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop the inner sense (Know Thyself) — test of philosophic capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The postulate/test of philosophic capacity is the heaven-descended 'KNOW THYSELF' — philosophy requires an 'inner sense' or self-intuition which is both practical and speculative. Those lacking the philosophic organ will find philosophy unintelligible, 'a mere play of words and notions'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only those who can actualize this inner consciousness — who have disciplined the faculty of self-intuition — can acquire the 'philosophic imagination' and the 'sacred power of self-intuition'. Example anti-patterns: treating philosophy as mere verbal logic (like music to the deaf); expecting external images to supply the direction of inner sense as in mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy may legitimately employ postulates/primary intuitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy, like geometry, must often begin from a 'primary intuition' or postulate (a first productive act for the inner sense) rather than from a demonstrable proposition; this is necessary for philosophy to arrive at evidence when outward images cannot determine the inner sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with geometry: mathematician postulates point/line; philosopher must postulate the first construction for inner sense. Practical implication: accept some foundational postulates where demonstration is impossible but intelligibility is required. Anti-pattern: demanding complete demonstration for every first principle where the discipline requires a postulate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain rigorous separation of methodologies (objective vs subjective starts)
rubrics_metrics.description: When pursuing natural philosophy start from the objective and explain how the subjective supervenes; when pursuing transcendental/intelligential philosophy start from the subjective and show how an objective coincides. Each science's success depends on austere adherence to its own principles and careful exclusion of those of the opposite science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural philosophers should avoid subjective suppositions (occult qualities, spiritual agents, teleology); transcendental philosophers should avoid interpellation of objective explanatory hypotheses (e.g., reducing perception to brain pictures). Anti-pattern: mixing explanatory moves of one pole into the other, producing confusion or category errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use voluntary scientific skepticism to purify the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophic method requires a 'voluntary doubt, this self-determined indetermination' (as in Descartes) — an absolute and scientific scepticism to remove innate prejudices so that future certainty can be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is distinct from scepticism that doubts for its own sake; the aim is positive: 'in eo eram ut aliquid certi reperirem' — to discover something certain. Anti-pattern: scepticism as mere negative refusal without constructive aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy as unity of the practical and speculative — knowledge requires coincidence of subject and object
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy is 'the science of BEING altogether' and thus its primary ground is neither merely speculative nor merely practical but both; 'All knowledge rests on the coincidence of an object with a subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication for production/criticism: philosophical writing must address both the moral/practical and the theoretical/speculative aspects; evaluation of philosophical claims should test whether they secure this coincidence. Anti-pattern: treating philosophy as only moralizing or only abstract speculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis on truth: correspondence and types (Thesis I & II)
rubrics_metrics.description: THESIS I: 'Truth is correlative to being. Knowledge without a correspondent reality is no knowledge.' THESIS II: 'All truth is either mediate ... or immediate and original. The latter is absolute ... The former is of dependent or conditional certainty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical implication: when assessing a claim or creative-philosophical statement, ask whether it corresponds to a reality (correlative being) and whether the claim is an original/immediate intuition (A A) or derived/mediate (B A), with differing degrees of certainty. Anti-pattern: conflating derived assertions with absolute intuitive truths or claiming absolute status for mediate truths.
